title: Identity
specPoints: My personal world: identity and relationships

tips.title: Age takes avoir
tips.body: *J'**ai** quatorze ans.* French *has* its years rather than *is* them. *Je suis quatorze* is the error every examiner has seen a thousand times, and *ans* is never dropped — *j'ai quatorze ans*, always with the noun.

tips.title: Nationalities agree and take no capital
tips.body: *Je suis **anglais*** (a boy), *je suis **anglaise*** (a girl). *-ais → -aise*, *-ien → -ienne*. And unlike English, the adjective has **no capital letter**: *anglais*, *française*, *écossais*. The country keeps its capital — *l'Angleterre, la France* — the adjective does not.

tips.title: Je suis né, je suis née
tips.body: *Je suis **né** à Londres* if you are a boy, *je suis **née** à Londres* if you are a girl. It is *naître* in the perfect tense with *être*, so the participle agrees. Write the one that is true of you — and the same for *fatigué(e), content(e), sportif / sportive*.

tips.title: Je viens de, j'habite à
tips.body: *Je **viens de** Manchester* (I come from), *j'**habite à** Leeds* (I live in). *De* for origin, *à* for a town you live in. For a country: *j'habite **en** Angleterre, **au** Pays de Galles* — the same *en / au* rule as the events topic.

tips.title: Je m'entends bien avec
tips.body: *Je **m'entends bien avec** ma mère.* (I get on well with.) *Je ne m'entends pas bien avec mon frère.* One reflexive phrase covers every relationship question, and adding *parce qu'il / elle est …* turns it into a reason.

why.matters: Name, age, where you live, what you are like: this is the French of every first meeting, every form, every role play that begins *tell me about yourself*, and every picture task that asks who the people are. It runs on two verbs, *être* and *avoir*, and it teaches the habit that will earn accuracy marks for two more years: agreement. A girl writes *je suis née* and *je suis anglaise*; nationalities take no capital; age is something you have, *j'ai quatorze ans*, not something you are. The topic is short, and its rules never stop applying.

examples.title: The form at the campsite
examples.body: A French form asks for *nom*, *prénom*, *âge*, *nationalité* and *adresse*, in that order, and the exam's role play asks the same questions out loud. *Nom* is your surname and *prénom* your first name, which trips English speakers who read *nom* as *name*. Nationality goes in with no capital and the right ending, and the date of birth is written with the day first. Fill it in once in your head and the introduction in any exam task is ready.

visual.alt: A table of the fields on a French form, nom, prénom, âge, nationalité and date de naissance, with what to write in each and the trap to watch

examples.title: Age is something you have
examples.body: English says *I am fourteen*; French says *I have fourteen years*, *j'ai quatorze ans*, and both halves matter. *Je suis quatorze* is the error that tells an examiner a candidate is translating, and dropping *ans* is the other. The same verb turns up in *j'ai faim*, *j'ai froid* and *j'ai peur*, so the habit pays beyond birthdays: when English says *I am* about a state, check whether French says *I have*.

props.title: When I am becomes I have

visual.alt: A table of English sentences beginning I am and their French versions, showing which take avoir, such as age and hunger, and which take être and agree

examples.title: The e nobody hears
examples.body: *Né* and *née*, *anglais* and *anglaise*, *paresseux* and *paresseuse*: the written form says who is speaking, and in most of these pairs the ear cannot tell. That is exactly why the writing paper and the dictation test them. Agreement with *être* is the grammar being marked whenever you describe a person, yourself included, and it is a mark you can bank before you know a single hard word.

steps.title: Qui suis-je ?
steps.body:
Personal information is the first thing any conversation or role play asks for, and it runs on **être** and **avoir**.

**Name**: *je m'appelle Sam*, *mon nom de famille, c'est Patel*, *mon prénom, c'est Aisha* (first name).

**Age**: *j'**ai** quatorze ans* — with **avoir**, and always with *ans*. *Mon anniversaire, c'est le douze mai.*

**Birth**: *je suis né(e) en 2012 à Birmingham* — *naître* in the perfect tense with *être*, so a girl writes *née*. Someone born in 2012 is 14 in 2026.

**Where**: *j'habite à Leeds, dans le nord de l'Angleterre*. *Je viens de Londres* (I come from). *J'habite en Angleterre / en Écosse / au Pays de Galles / en Irlande du Nord.*

**Nationality**: *je suis anglais(e), écossais(e), gallois(e), irlandais(e), britannique, français(e), indien(ne), pakistanais(e), polonais(e), nigérian(e)*. Adjectives agree and take **no capital**.

**Languages**: *je parle anglais et un peu de français. À la maison, on parle ourdou / polonais / gallois.* Languages are masculine nouns with no article after *parler*.

steps.title: Ma personnalité
steps.body:
Describing yourself is **être + adjective**, and the adjective **agrees** with you.

*Je suis sympa, timide, bavard(e)* (chatty), *sportif / sportive, paresseux / paresseuse* (lazy), *travailleur / travailleuse* (hard-working), *drôle, gentil / gentille* (kind), *sérieux / sérieuse, intelligent(e), têtu(e)* (stubborn), *généreux / généreuse*.

**Agreement patterns**: add *-e* (*bavard → bavarde*); *-if → -ive* (*sportif → sportive*); *-eux → -euse* (*paresseux → paresseuse*); *-eur → -euse* (*travailleur → travailleuse*); *-il → -ille* (*gentil → gentille*); *-e* stays (*timide, drôle, sympa*).

**Softening and strengthening**: *assez* (quite), *très* (very), *un peu* (a bit), *trop* (too): *je suis assez timide mais très sympa*.

**Contrast**: *je suis sportif mais un peu paresseux le week-end*. *Mais* between two adjectives is the simplest way to sound balanced.

**What others say**: *mes amis disent que je suis drôle* (my friends say that I am funny). *Disent que* + a full clause is a higher-band structure.

**Character and interests together**: *je suis sportif et je fais du foot* — a trait, then the evidence.

steps.title: Ma famille et mes relations
steps.body:
**The family**: *ma mère, mon père, mes parents, mon frère, ma sœur, mon demi-frère* (half-brother or stepbrother), *ma demi-sœur, mon beau-père* (stepfather), *ma belle-mère, mes grands-parents, mon oncle, ma tante, mon cousin, ma cousine*. *Je suis fils / fille unique* — an only child.

**Possessives agree with the noun, not the owner**: *mon père, ma mère, mes parents* — and *mon* before a feminine noun starting with a vowel: *mon amie*.

**Family shape**: *il y a cinq personnes dans ma famille. J'ai deux frères et une sœur. Mes parents sont divorcés / séparés. J'habite avec ma mère et mon beau-père.*

**Getting on**: *je **m'entends bien avec** ma sœur* (I get on well with), *je **ne m'entends pas bien avec** mon frère*, *on se dispute* (we argue), *on s'amuse bien ensemble* (we have fun together).

**Reasons**: *parce qu'elle est gentille, parce qu'il est trop sérieux, parce qu'on a les mêmes goûts* (the same tastes), *parce qu'il m'énerve* (he annoys me).

**Describing a relative**: *ma mère s'appelle Anna, elle a quarante ans, elle est infirmière et elle est très patiente.* Same structures as for yourself, in the third person — *il / elle est*, *il / elle a*.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Write your name, age and birthday in French.
2. Write where you were born and where you live, with *né(e)* and *à*.
3. Give your nationality with the correct agreement and no capital.

**Part B.**

4. Describe your personality with three adjectives, one softened with *assez* or *un peu*.
5. Say which languages you speak, and which are spoken at home.
6. List the people in your family with the right possessives.

**Part C.**

7. Say who you get on well with and why.
8. Say who you argue with and why.
9. Write a paragraph of six sentences introducing yourself and one family member.

For question 9, every adjective agrees with the person it describes.

rows: je suis né(e) à …, j'habite à …
je m'entends bien avec … parce que

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Age with avoir, and keep ans.** *J'ai quatorze ans.* Nothing else.

**Agree everything with the right person.** *Je suis née* (a girl), *mon frère est paresseux, ma sœur est paresseuse*. Agreement with *être* is the grammar being marked in a description, and it applies to nationality, personality and participles alike.

**No capital on nationalities and languages.** *Je suis anglaise, je parle français.* An English habit that marks the answer as translated.

**Possessives follow the noun.** *Mon père, ma mère, mes parents, mon amie.* Never *ma amie*.

**Use d'origine.** *Je suis britannique d'origine pakistanaise* — nationality and heritage in one line, with two agreeing adjectives.

**Give relationships a reason.** *Je m'entends bien avec ma tante parce qu'elle est généreuse et qu'on a les mêmes goûts.* Note *et qu'* — a second reason after *parce que* repeats *que*.

**Report what others think.** *Mes profs disent que je suis travailleuse, mais mes parents pensent que je suis un peu têtue.* *Dire que* and *penser que* plus a clause is range.

**Describe a relative with the same kit.** Name, age, job, personality, in the third person — *elle s'appelle, elle a, elle est*. It doubles the content of a Year 9 answer without new vocabulary.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- *Je m'appelle …, mon prénom, mon nom de famille*.
- **Age with avoir**: *j'ai quatorze ans*.
- *Mon anniversaire, c'est le … *.
- *Je suis né / née à …* — *naître* with *être*, agreement.
- *J'habite à* + town, *en / au* + country; *je viens de*.
- Nationalities **agree** and take **no capital**: *anglais(e), gallois(e), indien(ne)*.
- *Je parle anglais* — no article after *parler*.
- Personality: *être* + adjective, agreeing: *sportif / sportive, paresseux / paresseuse, gentil / gentille*.
- *Assez, très, un peu, trop* + adjective; *mais* for contrast.
- *Mes amis disent que je suis …*
- Family: *mon, ma, mes* follow the noun; *mon amie*.
- *Je m'entends bien avec … parce que …*
- *On se dispute, il m'énerve, on a les mêmes goûts*.
- *D'origine* + nationality for heritage.

visuals.alt: A summary table of vocabulary and structures for talking about identity and family

questions.prompt: Why is it **mon amie** for a female friend, when *amie* is feminine?
options: Amie is treated as masculine when it follows a possessive
Ma becomes mon before a vowel to avoid two vowels together

questions.solution: *Ma* + vowel would put two vowels together, so French uses **mon** before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or silent *h*: *mon amie, mon histoire*. The noun stays feminine: *mon amie est gentille*.

examTechnique.body:
Give the personal details in the fixed shapes — **j'ai … ans**, **je suis né(e) à**, **j'habite à / en / au**, **je suis + nationality** with agreement and no capital, **je parle + language** with no article.

Describe personality with agreeing adjectives, an intensifier and *mais*; describe relationships with *je m'entends bien avec … parce que …*, and describe one relative in the third person.
examinerErrors: Né for a girl, née for a boy.
Adjectives not agreeing with the speaker.
Every sentence in the first person.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gets every fixed structure right — *j'ai quatorze ans, je suis née à, j'habite en* — and agrees every adjective and participle with the person it describes, nationalities included, with no stray capitals. It adds *d'origine* for heritage, reports what others say with *disent que*, gives two reasons with *et que*, and describes a relative in the third person with the same kit.
